object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: The customer entity in the system; every account has an account number and everything hangs off it.

source_references.excerpt: An account. Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off.

object_types.name: AccountNumber
object_types.definition: Six digit, sequential, never reused identifier for an account.

source_references.excerpt: Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: One of the company's products, identified by a product code.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: ProductCode
object_types.definition: Identifying code for a product.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: PricePlan
object_types.definition: The billing artefact that says what the customer pays and how often; generates the invoice line.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: PlanCode
object_types.definition: Identifying code for a price plan.

source_references.excerpt: CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: FeatureBundle
object_types.definition: The feature bundle the customer gets - Starter, Professional, Enterprise - identified by its name.

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle
Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me. ... Is the name unique? ... Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: FeatureBundleName
object_types.definition: Unique name of a feature bundle.

source_references.excerpt: Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: The agreement that this account pays this amount on this cycle for this thing; identified by a subscription ID.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID.

object_types.name: SubscriptionId
object_types.definition: Unique, generated identifier for a subscription, prefixed with SUB.

source_references.excerpt: Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: StartDate
object_types.definition: The date a subscription starts; always present, mandatory.

source_references.excerpt: Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: EndDate
object_types.definition: The date a subscription ends; optional, present only for fixed-term or cancelled subscriptions.

source_references.excerpt: An open-ended subscription has no end date. Most of them are open-ended -- they run until cancelled. A fixed-term one has an end date agreed up front, that's usually an enterprise deal.

object_types.name: BillingPeriod
object_types.definition: The billing cycle of a subscription: monthly or annual.

source_references.excerpt: Monthly or annual.

object_types.name: SubscriptionStatus
object_types.definition: The status of a subscription: trialing, active, past due, or cancelled.

source_references.excerpt: Trialing, active, past due, cancelled.

object_types.name: PausedFlag
object_types.definition: A separate boolean flag indicating a subscription is paused; not part of the status enum, overlaps confusingly with active status.

source_references.excerpt: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag. ... It behaves like a status but it isn't one, it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs.

object_types.name: PlanChange
object_types.definition: A record of a change of price plan on a subscription, with its own identity, effective date, requester and target price plan.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record. We don't overwrite the plan on the subscription, we write a plan change with an effective date... It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: ChangeId
object_types.definition: Unique identifier of a plan change record.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: EffectiveDate
object_types.definition: The date on which a plan change takes effect.

source_references.excerpt: Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.

object_types.name: Requester
object_types.definition: The person who requested a plan change.

source_references.excerpt: It records the subscription, the new price plan, the effective date, and who requested it.

object_types.name: MRR
object_types.definition: Monthly recurring revenue; derived from the price plan's price normalised to a month, not stored.

source_references.excerpt: Every subscription has an MRR. Monthly recurring revenue. ... It's worked out. It's the plan price normalised to a month.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record. We don't overwrite the plan on the subscription, we write a plan change with an effective date, and the subscription's current plan is derived from the change history.

ambiguities.description: The word 'plan' is used for three distinct concepts: the price plan (billing artefact), the feature bundle (product entitlement), and the sales-negotiated deal. The model captures the first two as PricePlan and FeatureBundle but the sales 'deal' concept was explicitly deferred to a different meeting and is not modeled at all. Clarify whether the sales deal concept needs to be represented in this model.

source_references.excerpt: So we've got two things both called plan. ... We've got two things both called plan, and the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated, which frequently matches neither.

ambiguities.description: Account identity: Priya states company name is explicitly NOT an identifier (duplicates exist) and email belongs to a 'contact' not the account. However, 'contact' as a concept was never modeled -- is there a Contact entity related to Account that should be captured?

source_references.excerpt: Is there anything else that identifies an account? Email, company name? ... Company name absolutely not, we have four accounts called "Acme." Email is on the contact, not the account.

ambiguities.description: When an account closes and the same company returns, they get a new account number and are treated as a new customer for reporting purposes, even though from a product perspective it's the same company. This means there is no entity-level concept of 'Company' distinct from Account in the current model, which may lose history. Should a Company concept exist above Account to preserve continuity?

source_references.excerpt: If an account closes and the same company comes back, they get a new number and we treat them as a new customer for reporting. ... Which drives me mad, incidentally, because from a product perspective it's the same company and we lose the history.

ambiguities.description: The 'Paused' flag on subscriptions overlaps confusingly with the Status value (especially 'Active'), and stakeholders acknowledge this causes bugs (querying active subscriptions returns paused ones too). It's unclear whether Paused should be modeled as a fifth status value, a true independent boolean, or a constraint should exist restricting when it can be true (e.g., only when status=Active). The transcript explicitly avoids inventing a fifth status, but the interaction between PausedFlag and SubscriptionStatus is left unresolved.

source_references.excerpt: There's also paused. ... It behaves like a status but it isn't one, it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs. If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too. ... I'm not going to invent a fifth status you don't have.

ambiguities.description: Mid-term cancellation policy on annual subscriptions for refunds is explicitly undecided and parked -- the current system behavior (no refund mechanism, end date set to paid-through date) is documented, but whether prorated refunds, credits, or run-to-term is the actual business rule is unresolved by finance and legal. This is a known open constraint gap.

source_references.excerpt: Is there a rule today that I could write down? ... What happens commercially when an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term -- run to term, prorated refund, or credit -- is undecided.

ambiguities.description: The relationship between the manual credits/refunds (the 'Halloway'-style goodwill credits mentioned by Tom, four times last quarter) and the Subscription/PlanChange model is not captured -- no entity for 'Credit' or 'Refund' exists even though they are referenced as real business events. Should a Credit/Refund entity be modeled?

source_references.excerpt: It becomes one when the customer escalates and we give them a refund anyway, which we did four times last quarter. ... the four Tom's talking about were manual credits raised outside the subscription.

ambiguities.description: The current price plan on a Subscription is a denormalised field maintained by the change process, and is stated to be derivable from PlanChange history, yet it is also treated as a stored, potentially disagreeing field ('if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug'). This creates tension in the model: should CurrentPricePlan be modeled as a stored mandatory role (as captured) or purely derived from PlanChange with no stored attribute at all? The transcript settles on 'stored but should match derivation', which is an inherent redundancy the model does not fully resolve.

source_references.excerpt: No, Sam, it does have a current plan field. The changes are the history, but there's a denormalised current plan on the record. ... And if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug.

ambiguities.description: A fourth product is 'in discovery' but not yet defined or coded. The ProductCode value constraint of exactly three values (CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT) may need revisiting soon; this is noted as a temporal/completeness concern rather than a firm constraint.

source_references.excerpt: Fixed today. There's a fourth in discovery, but I'm not going to pretend I know what it is.
